current_episode.title: Women in Utilities Network: building careers through connection

guest.bio_context: Karen Anderson has been Executive Director of the Women's Utilities Network for just over two years. She actively speaks at industry events, including the Future Utilities conference, where she engages with large audiences on gender diversity in the utilities sector.

context.real_quote: Mentoring, for me, has given me a purpose. Seeing people build confidence, overcoming obstacles, they've set goals that they thought were impossible. Seeing them achieve those goals has been rewarding.
key_stats: Women's Utilities Network founded in 2018 by five women in the utilities sector
The network has grown over 8 years since its founding

pending_qa.q: How can professionals approach networking in a less daunting, more authentic way?
pending_qa.r: Sophia Goring advises going into networking with an open mind about potential value, without putting too much pressure on yourself, since some opportunities will come to nothing but others can open up career opportunities or new friendships. She notes that labelling a conversation as 'networking' makes people nervous, whereas simply having a genuine conversation — as people do every day — removes that pressure.

pending_qa.q: How did networking directly shape Sophia Goring's career path into sustainability?
pending_qa.r: Sophia Goring met a woman named Lindsay who worked for a social mobility charity called Career Ready while she was working in communications. That conversation led Business Stream to bring Career Ready in as a partner, sparked Sophia's interest in social value, and ultimately led to her moving into the role of heading up the sustainability team at Business Stream.

pending_qa.q: What do mentors gain from mentoring relationships, beyond what mentees receive?
pending_qa.r: Both Naz Khanon and Sophia Goring emphasise that mentoring is a two-way relationship: mentors develop coaching skills, broaden their understanding through others' experiences, and gain a sense of purpose by seeing mentees achieve goals they thought were impossible. Sophia also notes that mentees have shared perspectives that made her reconsider things she had never considered before, and that she genuinely builds friendships through the process.

pending_qa.q: How does mentoring help with imposter syndrome in the workplace?
pending_qa.r: Naz Khanon acknowledges that imposter syndrome is something many people suffer with, and that mentoring helps by constantly checking, improving and questioning oneself — which she and the host reframe as a potential superpower. The act of being a mentor also reinforces confidence, as people come to Naz as a member of the senior leadership team seeking support, which itself validates her expertise.

pending_qa.q: What is the One Mentoring Programme and how does it help people find mentors?
pending_qa.r: The One Mentoring Programme is described as a portal that connects mentors and mentees across the utilities industry, including outside of one's own organisation or line of work, providing unbiased support from someone with a completely different viewpoint. Both Sophia Goring and Karen Anderson highlight it as a structured route to finding mentorship, complementing informal mentoring relationships that can also develop throughout a career.

pending_qa.q: Why is diversity of backgrounds and perspectives important for utilities companies?
pending_qa.r: Karen Anderson argues that a utilities workforce needs to reflect its diverse customer base, and if everyone in a team looks, thinks and acts the same, the organisation fails to represent the people it serves. Naz Khanon adds that people from different backgrounds bring unique voices, opinions and stories that allow teams to tap into each other's strengths, while Sophia Goring notes that diversity of people drives diversity of ideas needed to address major industry challenges such as climate change and water pressures.

pending_qa.q: What career advice does the Women's Utilities Network panel offer to young people entering the utilities industry?
pending_qa.r: Sophia Goring encourages young people to be open-minded about the range of roles that exist in utilities — beyond the perception of only fieldwork — including communications, finance, and people teams. Naz Khanon advises not being afraid to be yourself, as unique traits and qualities are exactly what the industry needs, while Karen Anderson urges young people to build connections, have brave conversations outside their daily tasks, and remember that no one cares as much about their career as they do.

pending_qa.q: How can experienced professionals avoid feeling phased out, and what role does mentoring play?
pending_qa.r: Sophia Goring suggests that experienced professionals who feel they are being sidelined should explore mentoring as an option, because it forces reflection on where you are and where you want to go — something that otherwise gets sidelined in a busy working life. She also points out that working with younger people can be refreshing and that accumulated expertise and experience does not have to be static.

pending_qa.q: What role do female role models in senior leadership play in retaining women in utilities?
pending_qa.r: Sophia Goring cites Business Stream's female CEO, who is also a mother, as an example of how having visible role models in senior positions signals to other women that there is no ceiling to their progress. Karen Anderson adds that having people from all different walks of life in senior leadership positions influences the culture of organisations, making them places where people from all backgrounds can join, stay and thrive.
